title: 3 Common First-Day-Of-School Mistakes
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin identifies three subtle but common mistakes that undermine an otherwise well-prepared first day of school: talking too much, which causes students to tune out and form a negative first impression; being too serious, which relies on an undercurrent of intimidation that damages rapport even if it produces short-term compliance; and being too timid, which signals to students that the teacher doesn't have the conviction to truly enforce the classroom management plan. He recommends breaking information into digestible, interactive chunks, presenting behavior expectations as 'good news' rather than a stern warning, and delivering the plan with boldness and confidence. Linsin notes these mistakes are particularly insidious because they are difficult to notice in oneself in the moment. He closes by framing simple self-awareness of which mistake a teacher is most prone to as the best defense against making it.
points: Talking too much on the first day causes students to tune out and form a negative first impression that can seed future misbehavior.
Being overly serious relies on an undercurrent of intimidation that may produce short-term compliance but damages long-term rapport and leverage.
Being too timid about classroom management signals to students that the teacher lacks the conviction to actually enforce the plan.
Behavior expectations should be broken into digestible, interactive chunks and presented as good news rather than a stern warning.
These mistakes are hard to notice in oneself in real time; deliberate self-awareness beforehand is the best defense against making them.
quotes: But there is something about the first day of school that causes many teachers to behave in ways that undermine their best laid plans.
Talk too much and they’ll tune you out. They’ll form a negative impression of you and being in your class, which is the seed from which misbehavior grows.
But using fear, no matter how subtle the undercurrent, to coerce good behavior will only make your job more difficult—because it will very effectively sabotage your relationship with your new class.
They fear disappointing their new class so much that they tiptoe around their classroom management plan. They minimize its importance.
So teach it boldly. Be clear and confident. Show your students through your words, your passion, and your very presence that you will indeed fulfill your every promise.

The mistakes above are particularly insidious because they’re difficult to see in oneself. You look back a week later and think, “I was so prepared, and I did everything I wanted to do, yet why am I struggling?
